## Abstract

Classical molecular dynamics simulations of plasma-surface interactions were per-

formed of physical sputtering and reactive ion etching, with predictions based on several

force fields. In this paper, we focus mainly on SiO2 but include some results for Si sub-

strates as well. We compare predictions from these MD simulations to experimental

studies of SiO2 physical sputtering (by Ar+ ions), RIE of Si, and RIE of SiO2 (both

using F atoms and Ar+ ions). MD results using different published force fields are com-

pared to reported yields from published vacuum beam experiments. The near-surface

depth profiles predicted using different force fields are compared. One motivation for

the present study is to document the nature and magnitude of differences in the pre-

dictions for selected systems and conditions of practical interest.

## I. Introduction

One of the priority research opportunities (PROs) in the recently published report “Plasma

Science for Microelectronics Nanofabrication” is to develop, assess, and document fundamen-

tal data needed for modeling plasma-surface interactions.1 Molecular dynamics simulations

require accurate force fields or interatomic potential expressions for this purpose. One mo-

tivation for the present publication is to begin to document information for a MD plasma-

surface interaction database. In addition to publishing the details of the force field expression,

there is a need to assess their accuracy. When multiple force fields for the same materials

are available in the literature, results from the different models need to be compared. In

the present paper, we benchmark the MD simulation results by comparing to measurements

reported from vacuum beam experiments. Testing MD simulation predictions through com-

parisons to beam experiment data is convenient, in part because the beam experiments are

relatively simple and easily interpreted. Experiments performed on surfaces exposed to plas-

mas can be more directly relevant, but it is often the case that the composition and energies

2


<!-- Page 3 -->


of the multiple species impacting the surface are not known for the plasma environment and

this can affect interpretation of the results.

Silicon (Si) and silicon dioxide (SiO2) continue to be widely used in the semiconductor

industry. SiO2 is commonly used as a key dielectric material for devices based on Si. Within

the context of semiconductor processing and patterning, it is imperative to understand and

control etching processes at the atomic scale. Indeed there are many experimental studies

on the etching of Si2–8 and SiO2 9–23 especially using plasma. As semiconductor feature sizes

continue to shrink and devices become more sensitive to surfaces and interfaces, developing an

atomic-level understanding of plasma-surface interactions, etching kinetics, and the various

effects on surface structure has become increasingly important. This is especially true for

processing techniques such as atomic layer etching (ALE).24–28

Simulation techniques that provide insight into atomic-scale phenomena are indispensable

for building this understanding. Ab initio quantum mechanical calculations have been used

to study etching of both Si29–38 and SiO2.39–41 While ab initio calculations can provide

important information such as reaction pathways, these calculations can be computationally

expensive in the context of plasma-surface interactions. For example, one key issue is the

need to simulate enough impacts of plasma-generated species with surfaces to obtain a

steady state surface. On the other hand, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can

simulate relatively large systems (on the order of 1000s of atoms) for relatively long time

scales (on the order of several nanoseconds). However, reliable and useful predictions of

plasma-surface modifications from MD simulations require reasonably accurate force fields

used to describe interactions between atoms.

There exist many force fields in the literature used to study the etching of Si and related

materials by relevant plasma species. For example, there has been extensive work study-

ing the etching of Si by fluorine using ab initio-derived Stillinger-Weber force fields.34,42–44

A similar force field exist for silicon-chlorine interactions.45 Tersoff and reactive empirical

bond-order potential (REBO) force fields have also been developed to study Si etching by

3


<!-- Page 4 -->


fluorocarbons, fluorine, and chlorine.46–49

Several MD force fields for the interaction of SiO2 with gaseous and plasma species exist.

For example, Stillinger-Weber-type potentials developed by Watanabe et al.50 and Ohta

and Hamaguchi51 have been developed to model interactions of SiO2 with fluorine (F) and

chlorine (Cl) as well as fluorocarbon species.52,53 These force fields were extended to include

more species. For example, Cagomoc et al. used these force fields to study etching of

oxide-nitride bilayers.54 Tinacba et al. give force field parameters to simulate the etching

of SiO2 by SF+ 5 ions.55 Smirnov et al. also developed a similar model,56 although they only

provide parameters for Si, O, C, and F. More recently, Kim et al. developed a set of ReaxFF

potential parameters for SiO2 etching by HF.57

It is clear that there is not a lack of MD force fields available to investigate Si and

SiO2 etching by a variety of plasma species. With the advent of atomic-scale processing,

it is imperative that predictions from these models are rigorously compared to available

experimental data. Vacuum beam experiments are ideal for validating MD simulations

because it is known what species are interacting with the substrate. An example of this can

be found in our recent publication comparing MD predictions to vacuum beam experiments

of silicon etching by Cl and Ar+ ions49 and the aforementioned work by Tinacba et al.55

In this paper, we explore the performance of various classical MD force fields for Si

and SiO2 etching. Experimental results from published vacuum beam systems are used to

benchmark the performance of each model. We primarily investigate etching by fluorine (F)

and argon ions (Ar+). Depending on the substrate (Si or SiO2) and the incoming species

(F and/or Ar+) different force fields are examined. This is because all parameters used in

the force field expressions (e.g., cross interactions) are not available in all published MD

force fields. The force fields used for each specific case will be detailed in the next section.

The goal is to assess the robustness and transferability of the force fields and areas where

improvement can be made.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II will provide details of the MD simulations.

4


<!-- Page 5 -->


Results and discussion will be given in Section III. Finally, concluding remarks on our findings

and future work will be given in Section IV.

## II. Simulation Details

For the etching simulations performed in this work, a semi-infinite slab is constructed

where the atoms are placed in appropriate lattice positions. For Si, the diamond-cubic

crystal structure is used, while for SiO2 the α-quartz crystal structure is used. The lattice

parameters used for the crystal structures, roughly correspond to their values at ambient

conditions (300 K and 1 atm). Periodic boundary conditions are imposed in the lateral

directions (x and y directions). For the Si slab, the cell dimensions are 32.63 ˚A by 32.63

˚A by 43.44 ˚A. Due to the fact that the α-quartz crystal structure belongs to the trigonal

crystal system, the simulation box is non-orthogonal. For this material, the simulation box

is a parallelepiped. The simulation box can be fully specified with six numbers following the

LAMMPS documentation.58 The six numbers are lx, lx, lz, xy, xz, and yz. The values used

in the SiO2 simulation are a = 30.13 ˚A, b = 26.1 ˚A, c = 43.2 ˚A, xy = −14.7, xz = 0, and yz = 0.

Details on non-orthogonal simulation boxes can be found in the LAMMPS documentation.58

See supplementary material at [URL will be inserted by AIP Publishing] for a LAMMPS data

file containing the crystal structure of SiO2 α-quartz crystal structure. Above both slabs (in

the z directions) there is a vacuum space. The atoms in the bottom two layers of the crystal

structures are held fixed to prevent drift of the simulation cell. Etching is simulated as a series

“impact” simulations. During an “impact” simulation, a species of interest (in this work

either a F atom or an Ar+ ion) is placed in a random position (x and y position) above the

slab, outside the interaction distance. The species is then allowed to impact the surface of the

slab. Velocities of the incoming species are assigned based on whether they are categorized

as “thermal” or “energetic”. “Thermal” species have their velocities assigned based on a

Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at 300 K. Only velocities with a negative z-component are

5


<!-- Page 6 -->


considered to ensure the “thermal” species impacts the slab. Note that “thermal” species do

not hit the surface at normal incidence because the velocity components are sampled from

a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. “Energetic” species represent ions accelerated through

the plasma sheath (or an ion beam source) and are assumed to impact the surface at normal

incidence and at a single energy. We note that the ions are assumed to recombine via Auger

processes before impacting the surface and are therefore treated as energetic neutral species

in their ground electronic state.

Each “impact” simulation consists of a 3-ps long MD trajectory run within the micro-

canonical ensemble (constant number of particles, volume, and total energy). A timestep of

0.5 fs is used. During the MD run, the incoming species is allowed to impact the surface of

the slab, leading to surface modification and etching of atoms. Any cluster of atoms that is

desorbed from the slab are deleted once they cross the top z boundary of the simulation box.

After the microcanonical impact ensemble, the simulation cell is cooled to 300 K using a

Langevin thermostat.59 This is done because impacting species will introduce energy to the

slab and thus will increase the temperature. In order to collect statistically significant results,

suitable for comparison to the experiment, many impact simulations are run. The exact ion

fluence required to reach steady state depends on the system being simulated as well as the

etching conditions for each system. That is, the number of ion impacts required depends on

whether we are etching Si or SiO2. It also depends on whether we are considering physical

sputtering or RIE. Furthermore, ion energy and flux ratio will also affect this number. The

choice of interatomic potentials will also have an effect. Therefore, for each case, we would

monitor the etch yield as a function of ion dose and ensure that we have indeed reached a

steady state etch yield. That being said, for all cases examined in this work, we typically

see steady state is reached after approximately 2-3 monolayers of Ar+ bombardment, where

one monolayer is 1×1015 Ar+/cm2. Error bars for etch yields are calculated and represent

95% confidence intervals calculated from 3-5 independent simulations.

In this work, we will consider three systems: physical sputtering of SiO2 by Ar+ ions;

6


<!-- Page 7 -->


reactive ion etching (RIE) of Si by F atoms and Ar+ ions; and RIE of SiO2 by F atoms and

Ar+ ions. The force fields examined for each system are given in the following subsections.

A. Physical Sputtering of SiO2

For physical sputtering simulations, only Ar+ ions are exposed to the slab. As noted

above, Ar+ ions are assumed to neutralize before impacting the surface and so do not actually

carry a charge. For physical sputtering of SiO2 we compare the performance of the modified

Stillinger-Weber potential developed by Watanabe et al.50 and Ohta and Hamaguchi51 to

the Tersoff potential developed by Munetoh et al.60 The Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark (ZBL)

potential61 is used for all interactions with Ar+ ions. For these simulations, LAMMPS (23

Jun 2022 version) was used.62,63 It should be noted that the LAMMPS code was customized

to incorporate modified Stillinger-Weber potentials due to the fact that they are not native

to the LAMMPS code. It should also be noted that we have neglected a term that appears

in front of the pair-wise portion of the modified Stillinger-Weber potential. This was done in

order to make the implementation of the potential into LAMMPS simpler and allow the code

to run more efficiently. We believe neglecting this term does not significantly affect results

as we were able to reproduce potential energies of a variety of structures reported in the

original references. See supplementary material at [URL will be inserted by AIP Publishing]

for details on the term that was neglected and potential energy curves of the aforementioned

structures.

## B. Si-F-Ar Reactive Ion Etching

During RIE simulations, the surface of the simulation slab is sequentially bombarded with

“thermal” F atoms and “energetic” Ar+ ions at a specified flux ratio. For Si-F-Ar RIE we

again use the modified Stillinger-Weber potential developed by Watanabe et al.50 and Ohta

and Hamaguchi,51 again implemented in the aforementioned LAMMPS code. Once again,

the ZBL potential is used for all interactions with Ar+ ions. We also compare to simulations

7


<!-- Page 8 -->


using the reactive empirical bond-order (REBO) potentials as described by Humbird and

Graves.48 These simulations are performed using an in-house code instead of LAMMPS

because the specific form of REBO potentials developed by Humbird and Graves is currently

not implemented in LAMMPS. It should also be noted for the REBO simulations, Ar+ ions

interactions are described with the Moli`ere potential.64 This is similar to the ZBL potential,

so we don’t expect this to cause significant differences, at least for the ion energies used in

this work.

C. SiO2-F-Ar Reactive Ion Etching

SiO2-F-Ar RIE simulations are only performed with the modified Stillinger-Weber po-

tential developed by Watanabe et al.50 and Ohta and Hamaguchi.51 The other potentials

we considered do not have parameter sets for F (for the case of the Tersoff potential) or for

O (for the case of the REBO potential). Nevertheless, it is still important to compare the

modified Stillinger-Weber potential results to any available experimental data. Note that

from this point forward, we will refer to the modified Stillinger-Weber potential as the po-

tential described by Ohta and Hamaguchi for brevity. Although the Si-O interactions were

initially developed in the 1999 paper by Watanabe et al.,50 Ohta and Hamaguchi introduced

parameters for F and Cl, thus giving a more “complete” parameter set in the sense that

more atom types can be simulated.

## III. Results

A. Physical Sputtering of SiO2

Etch yields (i.e., the average number of atoms removed per incident ion) as a function

of Ar+ ion energy are given in Figure 1. Results are shown for the MD simulations using

the potentials described by Ohta and Hamaguchi51 and Munetoh et al.60 Various sets of

experimental data are shown as well. Both force fields give reasonable agreement with

8


<!-- Page 9 -->


experiments, especially given the spread in the experimental data. However, the Munetoh

et al. potential appears to underestimate the etch yield (relative to all experimental data

sets) at ion energies 125 eV and above. It should not be surprising that the two force fields

give quantitatively different values for the etch yields.

*Figure 1: SiO2 sputtering yield (number of atoms per incident ion) as a function of Ar+*

ion energy. Two sets of MD simulation results (open symbols) are shown: the modified Stillinger-Weber Si-O potential described by Ohta and Hamaguchi50,51 and the Si-O Tersoff potential of Munetoh et al.60 MD simulation results are compared to experimental data (solid symbols).65–68

Starting with the initially unaltered layer, Figure 2 plots the amount of Si and O atoms

etched as a function of Ar+ ion dose for the Ohta and Hamaguchi force field. The ion energy

is 150 eV. It is clear that O is more readily etched than Si. At steady state, the etch yield

of O is approximately twice that of Si, which is necessary to conserve mass at steady state.

However, it is interesting to observe that this is not the case during the initial transient.

9


<!-- Page 10 -->


Initially, the O yield is more than double that of Si in this region before converging to the

steady state result. As will be illustrated later, this initial transient is needed to create the

altered near-surface region that corresponds to steady state sputtering.

*Figure 2: Cumulative amount of Si and O sputtered as a function of ion dose for the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential.50,51 The ion energy is 150 eV. The slopes of the dashed lines represent the respective steady state sputtering yields for each atom type.*

In Figure 3a, the depth profiles of Si and O are shown after steady state is reached for the

physical sputtering simulation using the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential. This corresponds

to an ion dose of approximately 6.4 × 1016 Ar+/cm2. At the bottom of the cell (which

corresponds to the bulk of the material), the atomic density of Si and O correspond to

their expected bulk values (shown as dashed lines). The density of O is twice that of Si,

corresponding to the stoichiometry of the material. However, near the surface the ratio of the

atomic densities is close to 1:1. Given the intrinsically different sputtering probabilities of

each atom, the near surface region composition and structure must change so that at steady

state, 2 O atoms are sputtered for every Si atom sputtered. This is a relatively simple

example of a key aspect of plasma-surface interactions: the plasma generally dramatically

10


<!-- Page 11 -->


alters the surface region of the material. Any proper understanding of plasmas-altered

surfaces requires an appreciation of this important fact.

*Figure 3: Sub-figure (a) shows the atomic density of Si (blue solid line) and O (red solid line) as a function of cell height for the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential,50,51 corresponding to the case illustrated in Figure 2. The results are taken at the end of a 150 eV Ar+ physical sputtering simulation. The vertical dashed lines correspond to the expected bulk atomic densities for Si (blue dashed line) and O (red dashed line). Sub-figure (b) shows a side view of the simulation cell. Yellow spheres are Si atoms and red spheres are O atoms. Ar atoms are hidden. The snapshot was rendered in OVITO.69*

The cumulative amount of Si and O atoms sputtered as a function of 150 eV Ar+ ion

dose for the Munetoh et al. force field is shown in Figure 4. The plot is qualitatively similar

to Figure 2. However, the values for the steady state sputtering yields are different as is

seen in Figure 1. Note that the sputtering simulations using that Munetoh et al. force

field predicts reaching steady state at a lower ion dose relative to the Ohta and Hamaguchi

potential illustrated above.

11


<!-- Page 12 -->


*Figure 4: Amount of Si and O etched as a function of ion dose for the Munetoh et al. potential.60 The ion energy is 150 eV. The slope of the dashed lines represents the respective steady state sputtering yields for each atom type.*

*Figure 5a shows the atomic depth profiles of Si and O for the Munetoh et al. potential.*

Once again, the results are shown after an ion dose 6.4 × 1016 Ar+/cm2. The near-surface

region of the simulation cell and the region near the bottom of the simulation cell are similar

to the atomic depth profile shown for the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential. However, between

these two regions (at a height between 30 ˚A and 50 ˚A), there is a significant increase in the

density of oxygen for this potential. It is not obvious why this feature appears using the

Munetoh et al. potential and not in the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential. Apparently, for

this potential, the O atom depth profile seen in Figure 5 is necessary to satisfy the steady

state sputtering constraint of 2 O atoms lost per Si atom lost.

*Figure 5: Sub-figure (a) shows the atomic density of Si (blue solid line) and O (red solid line) as a function of cell height for the Munetoh et al. potential.60 The results are taken at the end of a 150 eV Ar+ physical sputtering simulation. The dashed lines correspond to the expected bulk atomic densities for Si (blue dashed line) and O (red dashed line). Sub-figure (b) shows a side view of the simulation cell. Yellow spheres are Si atoms and red spheres are O atoms. Ar atoms are hidden. The snapshot was rendered in OVITO.69*

We note that both force fields show that the ratio of Si to O in the very near surface

region is 1:1. This is expected given that the etch yield of O is higher than Si, as noted

above. This near-surface enrichment of the component with the lower sputtering yield in

the sputtering of a two-component material has been well established experimentally.70–72

This has also been demonstrated in previous work using MD simulations.73,74 As an aside,

we note that details of surface composition and structural changes induced by plasma could

affect the form of parameterized surface models.12

## B. Si-F-Ar Reactive Ion Etching

*Figure 6 shows the comparison of etch yields for Si-F-Ar RIE as calculated from the MD*

simulations and taken from the vacuum beam experiments of Gray et al.12 The MD results

using the Humbird and Graves potential show good agreement with the experimental results

for the range of flux ratios examined. We note that this agreement is observed for the limited

range of flux ratios studied in this work. It is possible the Humbird and Graves potential will

see worse agreement at high flux ratios due to overestimating the amount of spontaneous

etching by F atoms. A similar problem was observed and addressed for the Si-Cl REBO

potential in our previous work.49 The results using the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential are

lower than the experimental etch yields, especially at higher flux ratios. It is possible that the

degree of spontaneous etching by F atoms is underestimated for this potential. It is worth

noting that the “accuracy” of the force field may depend on the experimental conditions

and specific results chosen for comparison. For example, in the present simulations, etch

product composition, energy and angular distributions have not been recorded and compared

to measurements. It is certainly possible that one parameterized force field appears more

accurate in one set of comparisons but not in another.

C. SiO2-F-Ar Reactive Ion Etching

The calculated etch yields for the RIE simulations of SiO2 are shown in Figure 9. The

etch yields are compared to vacuum beam experiments reported by Gray et al.12 The etch

yields are given as a function of the flux ratio (F/Ar+) for 20 eV and 150 eV Ar+ ions. Etch

yields predicted from the simulations show good agreement with the experimental data at

20 eV, but appear to overestimate the etch yield for 150 eV by a factor of about 3.

## IV. Concluding Remarks

Classical molecular dynamics simulations of plasma-surface interactions were performed

in order to compare sputtering and reactive ion etching yield predictions using several force

fields available in the literature. In this paper, we focus mainly on SiO2 but include some

results for Si substrates as well. We compare predictions from these MD simulations to

experimental studies of SiO2 physical sputtering of SiO2 (by Ar+ ions), RIE of Si, and RIE

of SiO2 (both using F atoms and Ar+ ions).

19


<!-- Page 20 -->


We note that there are significant quantitative variations in experimental results as well

as in MD predictions using different force fields, as might be expected. One motivation for

the present study is to document the nature and magnitude of these differences for selected

systems and conditions of practical interest.

For physical sputtering of SiO2, we compared the performance of the Ohta and Hamaguchi

potential and the Munetoh et al. potential to experimental data. Both potentials give

reasonably good agreement with experimental etch yields. It should be noted that the

reported experimental yields can vary by a factor of 3 over the conditions we examined.

Both force fields show that there is a depletion of O atoms near the surface during physical

sputtering, reflecting the higher sputtering yield of O relative to Si. It should be noted that

the atomic density profiles using the different force fields differ quantitatively.

Si-F-Ar RIE simulations are performed using the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential and the

Humbird and Graves potential. The Humbird and Graves potential gives results for etch

yields that are in good agreement with vacuum beam experiments. The Ohta and Hamaguchi

potential give etch yields that are lower for this system. This could be due in part to the

fact that this potential may not predict the degree of spontaneous etching of Si by F atoms.

The atomic density profiles are similar for both potentials.

We only used the Ohta and Hamaguchi potential for simulations of SiO2-F-Ar RIE. The

other force fields examined in this work for SiO2 apparently have not yet been parameterized

to include O or F. Etch yields as a function of the flux ratio are compared to experimental

etch yields. The simulations show near quantitative agreement with the experiments using

20 eV Ar+ ions; however, they appear to overestimate the etch yields for the 150 eV ion

case. As seen in the physical sputtering case, the ratio of Si to O in the near surface region

is near 1:1. In the RIE case, there is also a significant amount of F present in the top few

monolayers.

The comparisons performed in this work help document the current state of classical

MD simulations for plasma-surface interactions. Multiple empirical potentials are currently

20


<!-- Page 21 -->


available in the literature for a subset of semiconductor materials and plasma species used in

etching processes. While many of these potentials perform fairly well in semi-quantitatively

reproducing beam experiment results, there are significant differences between predictions,

leading to uncertainty about quantitative accuracy. These uncertainties become more impor-

tant when considering atomic-scale processing such as ALE. These potentials also come in a

variety of functional forms such as Stillinger-Weber, REBO, ReaxFF, etc. It can be difficult

to identify which functional forms are preferred for different species or conditions. Extending

these functional forms to facilitate more complex mixtures, commonly used in plasma pro-

cessing, is an important future objective. Machine learning techniques are currently being

explored to extend the utility of classical MD force fields, e.g. DeepMD,75 among others.

Finally, there is apparently no single repository of available potentials commonly used

for plasma-surface MD simulations. In this work, some of the potentials were not publicly

available and either were implemented in “in-house” codes or had to be separately hand-

coded into LAMMPS. The community would benefit from the development of interatomic

potential repositories such as OpenKIM.76 Information on the performance of the potentials

(in the context of plasma-surface interactions) should be documented as well.1
